Calculation source

Question

How do discrete jumps change European option prices relative to a continuous-return benchmark?

Method

A compensated jump-diffusion model, evaluated through a conditional-lognormal Poisson series.

Interpretation

Holding diffusion volatility fixed adds jump variance. The matched-variance comparison helps isolate differences in distribution shape.

Limitations

Illustrative pricing assumptions, not calibration. A simulated path does not establish how well a model fits observed markets.

Working paper / 01 · September 2026

Option Pricing With Continuous and Jump Returns

Jie Lin · Independent portfolio study · Simulation research note

This note compares European option prices under a continuous-return model and a model that permits discrete jumps. A conditional-lognormal series computes jump-diffusion prices, while an independent Monte Carlo calculation checks numerical agreement. A second diffusion benchmark matches log-return variance to help distinguish the effect of total variance from the effect of the return distribution.

This paper reports a fixed, reproducible reference experiment. Changing the explorer above does not change the paper. The inputs are chosen pricing assumptions, not observed or calibrated market data.

1. Models and pricing measure

The diffusion benchmark assumes constant volatility, interest rate and continuous dividend yield. The jump model adds independent Poisson jump arrivals with normally distributed log jump sizes.

Diffusion: ST = S0 exp[(r − q − σ²/2)T + σ√T Z]
Jump diffusion: ST = S0 exp[(r − q − λκ − σ²/2)T + σ√T Z + ΣYi]
NT ∼ Poisson(λT), Yi ∼ Normal(μJ, δ²), Z ∼ Normal(0, 1)
κ = exp(μJ + δ²/2) − 1

The compensation −λκ adjusts for the expected proportional jump return, giving E[ST] = S0 exp[(r − q)T] under the selected pricing measure. Historical jump estimates do not automatically supply risk-neutral parameters. This study neither estimates a jump-risk premium nor infers a unique market pricing measure.

2. Conditional valuation and truncation

Conditional on n jumps, log terminal price is normal with mean an and variance vn. The discounted conditional payoff is weighted by Poisson(λT) probabilities.

an = log(S0) + (r − q − λκ − σ²/2)T + nμJ
vn = σ²T + nδ²
d2,n = (an − log K) / √vn,   d1,n = d2,n + √vn
Cn = exp(−rT)[exp(an + vn/2)Φ(d1,n) − KΦ(d2,n)]
Pn = exp(−rT)[KΦ(−d2,n) − exp(an + vn/2)Φ(−d1,n)]

Zero conditional variance uses a discounted deterministic payoff; expiry uses intrinsic value. With m = exp(μJ + δ²/2), omitted call terms after n = N are bounded by S0 exp(−qT) Pr[Poisson(λTm) > N]. Omitted put terms are bounded by K exp(−rT) Pr[Poisson(λT) > N]. The bound measures series truncation only, not floating-point or normal-CDF approximation error.

3. Reference experiment

ParameterValue
Spot / strike100 / 100
Maturity1 year
Rate / dividend yield4% / 1%
Diffusion volatility20%
Jump intensity0.5 per year
Mean log jump / log-jump volatility−0.05 / 0.15
Exercise / payoffEuropean call

First, hold diffusion volatility fixed and add jump risk. Second, compare a diffusion with σmatch = √[σ² + λ(μJ² + δ²)]. This matches annual log-return variance, but not skewness, tail behavior or all option prices.

Black–Scholes9.319738

At these assumptions, the Merton call is 0.975783 above the original diffusion baseline and -0.140071 relative to the variance-matched benchmark. Adding jumps does not imply the same price ordering against every benchmark.

4. Independent simulation check

An exact-terminal Monte Carlo implementation samples jump counts and log returns, then discounts the simulated payoff. It does not call the conditional pricing series. A fixed seed makes the estimate reproducible.

The series price lies within this simulation interval. Confidence intervals quantify sampling uncertainty; they are not deterministic error guarantees. Tests also check known diffusion values, European put–call parity, expiry, deterministic limits, price bounds and recovery of the baseline when jumps vanish.

5. Limitations and next research step

Constant parameters, independent normal log jumps and European exercise make the comparison tractable. The exercise excludes stochastic volatility, liquidity, transaction costs and early exercise. Simulated paths illustrate the model; they do not validate it against markets.

An empirical extension would document a dated option dataset, quote filters, rates and dividends, calibrate on one sample and evaluate later observations separately. Pricing errors and failed hypotheses should be reported alongside favorable findings. No historical fit, trading return or investment recommendation is claimed here.

References and reproducibility

  1. Black, F. and Scholes, M. (1973). The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities.
  2. Merton, R. C. (1975 working paper; published 1976). Option Pricing When Underlying Stock Returns Are Discontinuous.
